findings.title: Two near-simultaneous startUpload/uploadRun calls both pass the MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS gate
findings.scenario: Two requests (two browser tabs, two users, or a script) call startUpload/uploadRun within the same instant. Both land on request-handling threads inside the one uvicorn worker (Django sync views run on a threadpool under ASGI), so both call controllers._launch(). _launch() does `if _reap() >= MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS: raise IngestBusy` and only THEN appends the new Popen to the module-level `_running` list -- these are two separate, unlocked steps on a plain global list. With MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS=2 and one job already running, both threads' _reap() calls can each read len(_running)==1, both see 1 < 2, and both proceed to subprocess.Popen(...) + _running.append(...). subprocess.Popen releases the GIL across the underlying fork/exec syscalls, which widens this window well past a single bytecode gap. The result is 3 (or more, under a burst) concurrent ingest_archive subprocesses -- each holding the GIL through DuckDB/pandas per the module's own docstring -- on a host the code explicitly says serves on one uvicorn worker specifically to avoid this. There is no lock, semaphore, or atomic compare-and-append anywhere in this path.
evidence: controllers.py:459 MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS default 2
controllers.py:469-480 _reap(): global _running; iterate/poll a snapshot, then rebind `_running` from a filter over the current global -- no lock
controllers.py:495 `if _reap() >= MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS: raise IngestBusy(...)` -- check
controllers.py:510 `_running.append(subprocess.Popen(...))` -- act, in a separate statement, after Popen's fork/exec (GIL-releasing) has already run
No threading.Lock, Semaphore, or other synchronization primitive is imported or used anywhere in controllers.py
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the check-then-append in _launch() with a module-level threading.Lock (or replace the list+manual count with a threading.BoundedSemaphore sized to MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS, acquired non-blocking before Popen and tied to the child's lifetime for release in _reap()).

findings.title: Object-storage publish has no collision guard, unlike the local path fixed in this same diff -- two uploads of one run name can interleave objects under a shared prefix
findings.scenario: publish() checks `run_store.find(run_name) is not None` once, before extract+convert (which is minutes for a large run), then calls _publish_directory -> _upload_directory at the end with no re-check. For local storage this diff closes the gap by making the final `os.rename` itself the collision point: it fails with ENOTEMPTY when the destination is already populated, so 'two uploads of the same name can both pass that check before either writes' (the diff's own docstring) is handled. For object storage there is no equivalent: _upload_directory just PUTs every object and then manifest.json, unconditionally, with no exists-check, no conditional-put, no lock. Two jobs publishing the same run_name concurrently -- the ordinary case of a user re-submitting under an unchanged name after seeing a failure (either a genuine failure or the false-positive from _fail_if_stale, see companion finding), or simply two browser tabs -- both pass the early `run_store.find` check, then both walk their own converted output and PUT into the identical prefix `run_name/...`. Whichever writes manifest.json last makes the run 'appear' to the picker, but the object bodies underneath can be a mix of two independent conversions (different manifests, different catchment sets/schemas if the archives differ even slightly), and if job A's failure-cleanup (_delete_prefix) runs while job B is still uploading to the same prefix, A's listing-then-bulk-delete can remove B's freshly-written objects outright (see companion _delete_prefix finding).
evidence: ingest.py:183 `if run_store.find(run_name) is not None: raise ArchiveRejected(...)` -- checked once, long before publish

ingest.py:239-266 _publish_directory: local branch uses os.rename and treats OSError+exists as a real collision (the fix); object-storage branch just calls `_upload_directory(source, run_name)` with no equivalent check

ingest.py:268-306 _upload_directory: uploads `body` objects concurrently, then `tail` (manifest.json) -- nothing here checks whether the destination prefix already has content or is being written by another job

The diff's own docstring for _publish_directory states the local fix explicitly answers the same-name race ('this is the claim that the check in publish cannot make on its own') but does not extend that claim, or any mechanism, to the hosted branch
findings.suggested_fix: Before uploading, write a small sentinel object under the prefix using a conditional/if-none-match put (S3 supports `IfNoneMatch: '*'` on PutObject) to claim the run name atomically; on the object-storage path, re-check for an existing manifest.json immediately before writing the final manifest and abort (and clean up only your own objects) if one is now present.

findings.title: A job falsely declared stale-and-failed on the read side later succeeds -- the client has already stopped polling and never learns the true outcome
findings.scenario: _fail_if_stale is read-side only: read_status() synthesizes a FAILED document when `now - updated > STALE_AFTER_SECONDS` without writing anything back to storage. The subprocess writing real status (write_status, 'last write wins; there is one writer') is completely unaware. Since the docstring for STALE_AFTER_SECONDS itself notes 'progress is reported per stage, not per catchment' and a stage can legitimately run for the whole 30-minute window (e.g. _upload_directory pushing thousands of objects at UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY=16 over a slow link, with no intermediate `say()` call inside the upload loop), a job that is completely healthy but mid-way through one long stage gets reported FAILED to the client the moment it crosses 30 minutes since its last status write. uploadStatus marks that answer `terminal: true` (ingest.FAILED is in TERMINAL), and the frontend's poll loop in ngiab-upload-run.js returns as soon as it sees a terminal state -- it never polls that job id again. Meanwhile the real subprocess keeps running, finishes, and (for local storage, or for object storage if nothing else has since taken the name) successfully calls _publish_directory and writes state=DONE to the now-abandoned status object. The run is now live in the picker, but the user was told, authoritatively, that the upload failed and has no way to learn otherwise short of noticing the run appear on an unrelated page load.
evidence: ingest.py:133-159 _fail_if_stale: synthesizes `{**document, 'state': FAILED, ...}` and returns it -- comment explicitly says 'Read-side rather than written by anything'
controllers.py: uploadStatus sets `status['terminal'] = status.get('state') in ingest.TERMINAL` on whatever read_status returns, including the synthetic document

public/frontend/components/ngiab-upload-run.js _await(): loop returns on the first response where the status is terminal (pre-existing client behavior, unchanged by this diff) -- there is no re-poll after a terminal verdict
management/commands/ingest_archive.py:86-88 the real subprocess writes state=DONE unconditionally on success, with no check for whether it has already been externally declared dead
findings.suggested_fix: Have read_status write the synthetic stale-failure back to storage with a condition (e.g. only if `updated` still matches what was just read) so the verdict is decided once and the real writer can detect it was marked dead and skip publishing (or publish under a distinguishable name and log loudly); alternatively, have the frontend keep a low-frequency background check on a job it gave up on for a while and surface a reconciliation notice if the run appears anyway.

findings.title: Ingest scratch directories under the storage root's _uploads prefix are never swept when the child is killed before its finally block runs
findings.scenario: _workspace() now creates its scratch directory under `<local_root>/_uploads` (STAGING_DIR) instead of /tmp specifically so the final publish is a same-filesystem os.rename. Cleanup of that scratch directory is entirely `finally: shutil.rmtree(workspace, ignore_errors=True)` inside publish() -- code the ingest.py module docstring itself says a SIGKILL/OOM kill 'skips ... nothing writes a terminal status', i.e. also skips this finally block, since that's the same code path. There is no other sweep of `_uploads` anywhere in the codebase (grep confirms no cron, startup task, or management command touches STAGING_DIR besides ingest.py's own read/write of staging archives and status files). Because conversion is explicitly called out as 'the memory-hungry part' and the most likely cause of a kill, every OOM-killed large upload leaves a full extracted+partially-converted copy of that run permanently under `<local_root>/_uploads/ingest-*`, on the very filesystem that (per portal_config.yml) also hosts the sqlite database at /opt/ngiab. Repeated large-upload attempts that keep OOM-killing (a user retrying the same oversized archive, believing a transient failure) accumulate disk usage with nothing to reclaim it short of a manual operator cleanup or container restart wiping ephemeral storage.
evidence: ingest.py:52-59 STALE_AFTER_SECONDS docstring: 'A SIGKILL ... skips the command's except and finally, so nothing writes a terminal status'
ingest.py:219-237 _workspace(): local branch creates `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='ingest-', dir=staging)` under `run_store.local_root()/_uploads`
ingest.py:165-216 publish(): the only cleanup of `workspace` is the `finally: shutil.rmtree(...)` at the end of publish(), which does not execute on SIGKILL
grep across tethysapp/ngiab/*.py finds no other reference to STAGING_DIR or a sweep/cleanup task for orphaned entries under it
findings.suggested_fix: Add a startup or periodic sweep (e.g. in a Django app-ready hook or a small management command run from the container's entrypoint) that removes entries under `<local_root>/_uploads/ingest-*` and orphaned `<local_root>/_uploads/<job>/archive` older than STALE_AFTER_SECONDS, mirroring the staleness window already used to judge jobs dead.

findings.title: _delete_prefix's list-then-bulk-delete cleanup can remove objects a concurrent second uploader just wrote to the same prefix, and can miss just-written objects on non-strongly-consistent backends
findings.scenario: When _upload_directory fails partway, it calls run_store._delete_prefix(backend, run_name), which lists the prefix (_walk_keys -> backend.listdir) and then bulk-deletes whatever it finds. This is correct in isolation, but it is not scoped to 'the objects this job wrote' -- it deletes everything currently under the prefix at the moment of listing. Given the companion finding that nothing prevents two jobs from targeting the same run_name concurrently on the object-storage path, if job A fails and starts this cleanup while job B is mid-upload to the same prefix, A's listing can pick up B's already-written objects and delete them along with A's own, silently corrupting B's otherwise-successful publish. Separately, on any S3-compatible backend that is not strongly read-after-write consistent for LIST (the django-storages S3 backend is written against the generic boto3 client and the app explicitly supports arbitrary object storage via STORAGES, not only AWS S3), a listing taken immediately after a burst of concurrent PUTs can miss one of the objects this same job just wrote, leaving it behind after cleanup claims to have removed 'the partial run'.
evidence: run_store.py:505-538 _delete_prefix: lists the prefix via _walk_keys (backend.listdir) and deletes every key found, with no filtering to keys this call itself uploaded and no version/etag check

ingest.py:268-306 _upload_directory calls `run_store._delete_prefix(backend, run_name)` on any upload failure, scoped only by run_name, the same prefix a concurrently-racing second job (see companion finding) would also be writing to

ingest.py's own docstring for _upload_directory asserts 'the partial objects are removed on the way out' as an unconditional guarantee, which the listing-based approach cannot make on a backend without strong list consistency
findings.suggested_fix: Track and delete only the specific keys this call itself uploaded (the `body`/`tail` lists already built in _upload_directory) rather than re-listing the prefix; that also removes the same-prefix collision hazard since a failing job would never touch objects it did not itself write.

residual_risks: MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS and _running are process-local; the docstring at controllers.py:456 acknowledges this is 'the same granularity the rest of this module's process-local state already has,' but nothing in the shipped portal_config.yml enforces ASGI_PROCESSES=1 at deploy time, so the memory/GIL protection this commit adds is silently multiplied by whatever process count an operator configures.

Verified empirically (duckdb 1.4.4) that a cursor obtained via connect() keeps working after the originating _base_connection() Python wrapper is garbage collected, so duckdb_conn.reset() clearing the lru_cache while another thread holds an in-flight cursor from the old connection does not appear to crash or corrupt that in-flight query -- flagged here as checked-and-not-reproduced rather than as a finding.

run_store._cached_listing's ThreadPoolExecutor over _describe, and _describe's call to storage() (which builds a fresh backend instance per call rather than sharing one), do not share mutable state across threads -- each call constructs its own backend object -- so no cross-request corruption hazard was found there, only the already-known per-call construction cost.
testing_gaps: No test exercises two concurrent startUpload/uploadRun calls against a live (non-mocked) _launch to demonstrate the MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS TOCTOU window under real thread scheduling.

tests/test_publish_atomicity.py should be checked for whether it covers the object-storage (_upload_directory) branch's same-name race at all, versus only the local os.rename branch that this diff explicitly hardened.
No test simulates a job crossing STALE_AFTER_SECONDS and then the underlying subprocess completing successfully afterward, to confirm what the client and stored status end up showing.
